summary: This standards-track document describes how OSPF can gracefully take a link out of service. Raising the metric on one side is not enough to divert traffic flowing in the other direction. The mechanism lets routers on both ends of the link divert traffic before it is shut down.

eli5.summary: Before closing a two-way road, both ends must put up signs. This makes sure both sides tell traffic to go elsewhere before the road closes.

questions: how to gracefully shut down an ospf link
why is raising the ospf metric not enough
what is the ospf graceful link shutdown sub-tlv
subtitle: How an OSPF router warns both ends of a link, and any controller, that the link is about to go down for maintenance.

tldr.problem: Raising the metric on one side of a link does not divert the traffic flowing in the other direction, and changing metrics by hand on many links in both directions is tedious.
tldr.mechanism: The router with the link to be taken out of service advertises a Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV and sets its own metric to MaxLinkMetric (0xffff). The router at the other end sees the sub-TLV and raises its own metric for the link too.
tldr.outcome: Traffic is steered away from both directions, yet the link stays usable as a last resort if no other path exists. This RFC is updated by RFC 10041.

today: RFC 8379 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 10041. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Raising One Metric Is Not Enough
sections.content:
OSPF routers pick paths by adding up link metrics. When a link is about to be taken down for maintenance, an operator can raise the metric on one end, but that only affects traffic leaving from that end. Traffic flowing the other way still uses the link. The abstract states this plainly: increasing the metric to the highest value on one side is not sufficient.

The RFC also targets overlay networks built on pseudowires or L2 circuits. The routers underneath are invisible to OSPF, so the existing stub-router mechanism in RFC 6987 cannot be used. A single provider edge router may carry many customer-to-customer connections, and changing the metric on each one in both directions is cumbersome.

The stated objectives are to advertise the impending maintenance so traffic can be diverted from both directions, to stay backward compatible so that nodes which do not understand the new advertisement do not cause routing loops, to let traffic-engineering ingress routers and controllers learn about the maintenance, and to keep the link usable as a last resort when no alternate path exists.
sections.eli5: If only one side of a bridge puts up a 'closed' sign, cars from the other side still drive onto it. Both sides need to tell people, without needing anyone to visit every bridge by hand.

sections.title: Flooding the Shutdown Signal
sections.content:
The signal is a Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV that describes a link as being gracefully shut down. It is flooded through the OSPF area as part of the link's description, so every router in the area, including head-end routers and controllers, can see it.

  • In OSPFv2 it goes in the Extended Link TLV of an area-scoped Extended Link Opaque LSA, as defined in RFC 7684.
  • In OSPFv3 it goes in the Router-Link TLV of an E-Router-LSA, as defined in RFC 8362.

Because the information is a property of the link, a head-end or controller can use it as an explicit warning. The RFC points out that a higher metric alone does not say why the metric changed, since it could also rise for other reasons such as LDP-IGP synchronization.
sections.eli5: The router writes a note saying 'this road is closing soon' and passes it to everyone in the neighbourhood, so every driver and the traffic planners all hear about it.

sections.title: The New Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV has no value at all, only a type and a length of 0. It is type 7 in OSPFv2 and type 8 in OSPFv3.

Two optional OSPFv2 sub-TLVs help identify the exact link:

  • Remote IPv4 Address (type 8, length 4) carries the address of the far end of the link.
  • Local/Remote Interface ID (type 9, length 8) carries 4 octets of the Local Interface ID followed by 4 octets of the Remote Interface ID, for parallel unnumbered links.

The RFC also defines a Graceful-Link-Shutdown TLV for BGP-LS (RFC 7752), type 1121, again with length 0 and no value, so that external entities can learn about the shutdown through BGP.
sections.eli5: The note is just a stamp that says 'closing'. Extra labels can say which of two side-by-side roads you mean.

sections.title: Telling Parallel Links Apart
sections.content:
Imagine routers A and B joined by two parallel point-to-point links. An Extended Link Opaque LSA describes a link by Link Type, Link ID and Link Data. For a link with address I.w on Router A, that is point-to-point, the Router ID of B, and I.w. A third node cannot tell from this which interface on Router B is at the far end, I.y or I.z.

To remove the ambiguity, the originator should add a Remote IPv4 Address sub-TLV carrying the far-end address. OSPFv3 does not need this, because its Router-Link TLV already holds the interface ID and the neighbor's interface ID, which identify the remote interface uniquely.
sections.eli5: If two doors connect the same two rooms, you need to say which door you mean. The extra label names the door on the other side.

sections.title: What Routers Do
sections.content:
The node with the link to be taken out of service MUST advertise the Graceful-Link-Shutdown sub-TLV. When the link is ready to carry traffic again, the sub-TLV MUST be removed and the LSAs readvertised, with the metric restored to its original value.

For a point-to-point link, the originating node MUST set the link metric to MaxLinkMetric (0xffff) and reoriginate its Router-LSA. It SHOULD set the Traffic Engineering metric to 0xffffffff and reoriginate the TE Link Opaque LSAs. A remote node that receives the sub-TLV MUST find its matching local link, set that metric to 0xffff and reoriginate its Router-LSA, and SHOULD do the same for the TE metric. When the originator purges the LSA or reoriginates it without the sub-TLV, the remote node restores the original metric values. In multi-topology deployments, the receiver SHOULD change the reverse-direction metric for all topologies that include the link.

For broadcast and NBMA links, all neighbors share one link, so the remote metric cannot be changed without hurting every path through it. Instead the two-part metric of RFC 8042 is used: the originator sets the Network-to-Router Metric to 0xffff. Point-to-multipoint and hybrid links work like point-to-point links, with the remote node finding the corresponding neighbor and setting its metric to 0xffff. For unnumbered interfaces, the Link-Data field holds the Local Interface ID, and the Local/Remote Interface ID sub-TLV MUST be advertised when there are multiple parallel unnumbered interfaces.
sections.eli5: When one side announces the closure, the other side also turns its own sign to 'very expensive'. On a big shared road with many neighbours, only the announcer changes its own price, so nobody else is hurt.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content: The RFC calls the mechanism fully backward compatible. Both the advertising node and the node at the remote end must support the extensions for traffic to be diverted. If the remote node does not support the capability, it will still use the link, but there are no other adverse effects. On broadcast links with two-part metrics, the backward-compatibility procedures of RFC 8042 apply.
sections.eli5: If the other side has not learned the new signs, it just keeps using the road. Nothing breaks, but the traffic is not steered away either.

sections.title: Where It Is Used
sections.content:
The RFC describes four settings.

  • Overlay networks: when a provider edge router goes down, customer edge routers mark their overlay links, and traffic in both directions moves off that router without per-circuit manual changes.
  • Controllers: a controller that takes part in the IGP can reroute LSPs away from the link, and may temporarily relax constraints if no alternate path satisfies them. The RFC's example uses a 10 Gbps bandwidth constraint and two 1 Gbps alternate links.
  • L3VPN and sham links: all links, including sham links, on a provider edge router can be set to the shutdown state without touching the remote configuration.
  • Hub and spoke: all links on a hub being maintained can be set to shutdown so spoke traffic moves away without spoke configuration changes.
sections.eli5: Phone companies, traffic planners and big hub networks can all use the same note to move traffic aside before repairs, without visiting every single site.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC uses existing OSPF packets and LSAs, so the authentication procedures of RFC 2328 for OSPFv2 and RFC 4552 for OSPFv3 apply. It states that it introduces no further security issues beyond those already discussed in RFC 2328 and RFC 5340.

IANA registered sub-TLV values 7, 8 and 9 in the OSPFv2 Extended Link TLV Sub-TLVs registry, value 8 in the OSPFv3 Extended-LSA Sub-TLVs registry, and value 1121 in the BGP-LS TLV registry.
sections.eli5: The note travels with the same locks and seals as all other OSPF messages, so it is as safe as they are.
